title: The Little Giraffe Who Forgot to Look Down
titleZh: 忘了低头看的小长颈鹿

summary: Gemma the giraffe calf has the longest neck in the herd, and she uses it to look at everything far away - the river two hills off, the first cloud of the rainy season. She never looks down, so she never sees Nim the field mouse or Tuck the old tortoise, whose path she steps over every single morning. Then a storm comes, and Gemma's hoof drops into a crack between two rocks and will not come out. With nobody tall enough to pull her free, she finally looks down - and finds a whole world at her feet, and two small friends who can do what no tall animal can.
moral: Gemma learned that a long neck can show you the whole horizon, but it is looking down that shows you the ones standing beside you. Being big, or fast, or clever, or tall is never a reason to stop noticing the small things and small people around you. Respect does not begin with the animals who are as big as you are. It begins with the ones whose eyes are lower than yours - and it starts with a simple, kind look.
moralZh: 吉玛明白了：长长的脖子能让你望见整条地平线，可只有低下头，你才看得见站在你身边的那一个个。长得高、跑得快、聪明、力气大，从来都不是不去留意那些小小的东西、小小的人的理由。尊重不是从和你一样高大的伙伴开始的，而是从那些眼睛比你还低的小生命开始的——而它只始于一次简单的、温柔的低头。

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: On the wide Acacia Plain, where the grass turns gold in November and the wind smells of dust and warm stone, there lived a young giraffe named Gemma. Gemma had the longest neck of any calf in the herd. And because her neck was so long, she could see the river two hills away, the smoke of a distant fire, and the very first cloud of the rainy season. She could see everything. Everything, that is, that was far away.

paragraphs.speaker: Gemma
paragraphs.text: (stretching her neck as high as it would go) "Otis! Otis, look! I can see the river from here. Two whole hills away! Can you see it? No. Of course you cannot. You are an ostrich. I am a giraffe."

paragraphs.speaker: Otis
paragraphs.text: (flapping his big useless wings) "I can see it perfectly well, thank you very much. I simply choose not to look."

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Down on the ground, where the grass was short and the shadows were cool, small things were happening. A field mouse named Nim was carrying a seed home. An old tortoise named Tuck was crossing the path very, very slowly. Gemma's long legs stepped over them both - and she did not see either of them. Not once.

paragraphs.speaker: Nim
paragraphs.text: (dropping her seed and jumping back) "Whoa! Watch it! That hoof was as big as my whole house!" (peering up, whiskers twitching) "She did not even stop. She did not even see me."

paragraphs.speaker: Tuck
paragraphs.text: (not hurrying, because tortoises never do) "Ah. When you live that high up, the ground is a very long way away. But being tall is no excuse for not looking down, little mouse. A head in the clouds still has feet in the grass."

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Gemma and Otis laughed all the way across the plain. "Did you hear something down there?" Gemma asked. "Something squeaky?" "Only grass," said Otis. And they laughed again.

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Now, that November was a dry one. Day after day the sun came up like a hot coin, the river shrank to a thin silver thread, and the grass cracked into little dry puzzles under everyone's feet. Then one afternoon the sky turned purple, and the wind began to push.

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: "Storm!" called the herd, and everyone ran. Gemma ran too - long legs, fast legs, her eyes fixed on the far hills where the rain was already falling. She was so busy looking far away that she never looked down. And that is how her front hoof came down into the narrow crack between two flat rocks, and stuck.

paragraphs.speaker: Gemma
paragraphs.text: (pulling hard, her voice going high) "It will not come out! Otis! OTIS! My hoof is caught!"

paragraphs.speaker: Otis
paragraphs.text: (running up, then stopping short) "I see it. I see it. But I cannot pull you, Gemma. My legs are for running, not for pulling, and my wings are no use at all." (a pause) "I will run and fetch your mother. Hold on. Do not go anywhere."

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: "Do not go anywhere," said the ostrich - and then he ran away as fast as an ostrich can, which is very fast indeed. And Gemma was left alone in the hot, still afternoon, with her hoof in a rock and the storm coming.

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: For the first time in her life, Gemma had nowhere to look but down. And down, she discovered, was full of things she had never seen: a beetle in armour the colour of a plum, a line of ants carrying a white petal home, a seed pod curled like a sleeping ear. And two small faces, looking up at her from the shadow of the rock.

paragraphs.speaker: Nim
paragraphs.text: (paws on her hips, whiskers trembling) "You are stuck."

paragraphs.speaker: Gemma
paragraphs.text: (bending her long neck all the way down, until her nose was almost in the dust) "I am stuck. Please - can you help me?"

paragraphs.speaker: Nim
paragraphs.text: "Why should I? For a whole month you stepped over me every single morning. You never once said good morning. You never once looked."

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Gemma was silent. The wind blew, the dry grass bent, and she thought about all the mornings she had looked at the far hills and never at her own feet.

paragraphs.speaker: Gemma
paragraphs.text: (very quietly) "You are right. I did not look. I thought the small things were not important, because they were small. I was wrong, Nim. I am sorry."

paragraphs.speaker: Tuck
paragraphs.text: (arriving at last, one slow step at a time) "Little mouse, being small is not a reason to be small-hearted. Come. Let us show the tall one what small things can do."

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: So Nim did what mice do best. She dug. Her tiny paws flew, throwing out the loose red soil from around the hoof, one small pawful at a time, until there was a hollow where there had only been rock.

paragraphs.speaker: Tuck
paragraphs.text: (bracing his hard round shell against the stone) "Now, giraffe. Do not pull against the rock. Pull against me. My shell is smooth, and it has carried a hundred years of weather. It will not mind one small hoof."

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Gemma pulled. Her long leg slid along the smooth curve of the old shell - and with a soft, dusty pop, her hoof came free.

paragraphs.speaker: Gemma
paragraphs.text: (stumbling forward, then turning round and round) "It is out! It is out! Oh - thank you. Thank you both." (a pause) "I do not even know your names."

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: Just then Mama Giraffe came thundering across the plain with Otis behind her. She stopped. She stared. Her daughter was standing in the middle of the path with her head bowed all the way to the ground, talking to a mouse and a tortoise as if they were the most important animals on the whole wide plain. Which, that afternoon, they were.

paragraphs.speaker: Mama Giraffe
paragraphs.text: (softly, to Otis) "Who freed her?"

paragraphs.speaker: Otis
paragraphs.text: (looking down at his own feet for the very first time) "The two she never saw."

paragraphs.speaker: Gemma
paragraphs.text: (lowering her neck until it lay almost flat, nose to nose with Nim) "Nim. May I ask you something? What does the world look like, down there?"

paragraphs.speaker: Nim
paragraphs.text: (grinning so wide her whiskers touched her ears) "Small. And very close. Would you like to see?"

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: So Gemma lowered her head, and Nim climbed up the long warm slope of her neck and sat between her ears. Then Gemma lifted her - up, up, up, higher than any mouse has ever been - and the whole golden plain opened out in front of them: the river, the hills, the first grey curtain of rain walking slowly across the grass.

paragraphs.speaker: Nim
paragraphs.text: (very quietly, holding on with all four paws) "Oh. It is beautiful."

paragraphs.speaker: Gemma
paragraphs.text: (smiling up at her) "Yes. And I would never have seen it properly if I had not looked down first."

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: From that day on, Gemma looked down every morning before she looked far. She learned the names of the ants, and the plum-coloured beetle, and the tree with the curled seed pods. And when the other young giraffes asked her why she was always staring at her own feet, she only smiled and said: "I am not looking at my feet. I am looking at my friends."

paragraphs.speaker: Narrator
paragraphs.text: So here is the secret, little one, before you close your eyes. A long neck can show you the whole horizon, but it is looking down that shows you the ones standing beside you. Being big, or fast, or clever, or tall is never a reason to stop noticing the small things and the small people around you. Respect does not begin with the ones who are as big as you are. It begins with the ones whose eyes are lower than yours - and it starts with one simple, kind look. Good night, little one. Sleep well.
